analysis:
Examined the three modified files: EngineV2Bridge+Events.swift (pump now takes a per-request stopStringScope and forwards it to matchedStopSequence), EngineV2Bridge+StopSequence.swift (scope parameter threaded through; scoped matching now picks the first candidate that alone stops at the same scan result), and EngineV2Bridge+Submission.swift (new stopStringScope parameter on both submitTokenized overloads; scope is nil for CBv2NativeBlockEngine, else the request scope or the model default).

Security relevance: stop-string scope only affects which stop candidate is reported in usage metadata (matchedStopSequence) and where stops apply during generation. I saw no change to encryption, attestation, authorization, cache scoping (cacheScope/cacheSalt), key handling, telemetry content or resource-release paths. The pump's resource release logic (KV budget, prefix cache staging completion, retirement wait) is unchanged. No new data egress: telemetry still carries fixed keys only. The T-041 prefix-cache surface is not touched.

Minor observations, not findings: the per-candidate StopHoldback rescans in matchedStopSequence are O(candidates x text length) on the terminal path only. Candidate count and output length are bounded by request controls, which are outside the supplied evidence (the validation of stop-string count and size upstream was not visible). Also, the new parameter is only passed in the pump call at head line 948 in Submission; the unseen remainder of the Submission file and callers that supply a request-level stopStringScope (e.g. ReasoningStopScope derivation) were not in the supplied evidence. How consumers set that scope, and whether a consumer could weaken it, is an integration question. The StopHoldback type's equality and ingest semantics are also outside the supplied evidence.

No concrete security regression was identified.
